title: Per-tenant embedding dimension via an article_embeddings / memory_embeddings side table
background: The embedding vector dimension is pinned by the column type in exactly two migrations: priv/repo/migrations/20260410022854_enable_pgvector_and_add_embedding.exs:25 (ALTER TABLE articles ADD COLUMN embedding vector(1536)) and priv/repo/migrations/20260709000000_create_memory_stores.exs:101 (memories). The HNSW indexes do NOT pin a dimension - lib/loopctl/repo/hnsw_index.ex:125 emits USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops) parameterized only by table name, so it inherits whatever the column type is. Application.get_env(:loopctl, :embedding_dimensions, 1536) (config/config.exs:16) exists but is a CHANGESET VALIDATION ONLY (article.ex:490,506; memory.ex:281) - changing it does not change the column type, so 1536 is effectively hard system-wide. This is the blocker reported in #409: a local embedding model with a different native dimension (nomic-embed 768, bge 1024) cannot be used at all. The 2026-07-15 draft proposed a deployment-level single dimension; that is reversed here because the user who filed #409 is a HOSTED tenant, and a deployment-level dimension would force them off the hosted service to get a local model.

story.as_a: a tenant whose privacy or cost constraints require a specific embedding model
story.i_want_to: choose an embedding model whose native dimension is not 1536 and have loopctl store and index those vectors correctly
story.so_that: I can run local or self-chosen embeddings on the SAME hosted instance, without forking to a self-hosted deployment

rationale: Moving the vector out of a fixed-width column onto a dimension-tagged side table is what makes per-tenant embedding models possible on a shared multi-tenant instance. It is the difference between 'loopctl supports local models if you self-host' and 'loopctl supports local models', which is the whole product question behind this epic.

acceptance_criteria.description: Vectors move to side tables article_embeddings(article_id, dim, embedding) and memory_embeddings(memory_id, dim, embedding), each tenant_id-scoped with RLS via the existing enable_rls/1 macro (repo/rls_helpers.ex:38-63, ENABLE not FORCE), and a unique constraint on (article_id) / (memory_id) so one row holds the current vector.

One PARTIAL HNSW index per distinct dimension in use (WHERE dim = N), created by an idempotent helper extending repo/hnsw_index.ex. Adding a new dimension creates its index without touching existing ones; no index is created for a dimension with no rows.

A tenant's dimension is derived from its configured embedding model, not set by hand, and is readable via the API/MCP. Writing a vector whose length disagrees with the tenant's recorded dimension is rejected with a legible error naming both values - never silently stored or truncated.

Search and recall join the side table and filter by the caller tenant's dimension, so a tenant NEVER sees or ranks against vectors of a different dimension. A cross-dimension similarity comparison must be impossible by construction (the query is dimension-scoped), not merely unlikely.

Backfill migration moves every existing articles.embedding / memories.embedding into the side table with dim = 1536, is resumable and batched (the corpus is large - see epic 27 scale work), and leaves the old column in place but unused until a follow-up drop. Zero behavior change for existing tenants: same results, same ranking.

Changing a tenant's embedding model (and therefore dimension) is supported via an agent-triggerable re-embed backfill that reports progress through the existing job/anomaly surfaces. It is documented as a one-time operation, NOT an online migration; stale-dimension rows are excluded from recall until re-embedded rather than being compared incorrectly.

Query performance on the hosted default (dim 1536) does not regress measurably versus the current single-column form. The added join is on an indexed FK; a benchmark or query-plan assertion documents the result.

test_cases.name: two tenants with different dimensions coexist and never cross-rank
steps: run semantic search as tenant B
expected_results: only tenant B's 768-dim vectors are considered
no error, no dimension-mismatch from pgvector
tenant A's rows are invisible (RLS) AND dimension-excluded

test_cases.name: partial HNSW index exists per dimension and is used
steps: EXPLAIN the semantic search query for each dimension
expected_results: each plan uses the partial HNSW index for its own dim
no sequential scan over the side table

test_cases.name: backfill is resumable and lossless
preconditions: articles and memories with existing 1536-dim embeddings
expected_results: every vector present exactly once at dim 1536

test_cases.name: wrong-length vector is rejected legibly
expected_results: rejected with an error naming expected 768 and got 1536

test_cases.name: tenant isolation on the side tables
expected_results: tenant B rows are not visible (RLS policy enforced)

technical_notes: Only two column definitions actually pin the dimension; the HNSW helper (repo/hnsw_index.ex:125) is dimension-agnostic and can be reused nearly as-is with an added WHERE dim = N predicate.

Keep :embedding_dimensions as the DEFAULT for a tenant with no explicit model, so existing config semantics survive; the changeset validations at article.ex:490,506 and memory.ex:281 must switch to validating against the TENANT's dimension, not the global config.
pgvector cannot compare vectors of different dimensions - it errors. That is a safety net, not the design: the query must be dimension-scoped so the error is unreachable in normal operation.
Do NOT drop articles.embedding / memories.embedding in this story. Land the side table + backfill first, verify in prod, drop in a follow-up so a rollback stays trivial.
Memories already use explicit (tenant_id, subject_id) predicates rather than relying on RLS alone (memory.ex:18-42) - preserve that pattern on memory_embeddings.
Watch index build cost: HNSW builds are expensive at corpus scale. Create partial indexes CONCURRENTLY and treat a new dimension's first index build as an operational step.
